stem: A 35-year-old woman comes to the office for an initial appointment due to ongoing, generalized abdominal pain, weakness, decreased appetite, and dizziness.  She says the pain is becoming intolerable and she constantly feels "weak all over."  She has experienced no weight loss, nausea, diarrhea, or constipation.  Over the past several years, the patient has been admitted to the hospital 3 times due to similar symptoms; no etiology for the pain has been identified despite extensive work-ups, including esophagogastroduodenoscopy, colonoscopy, and several CT scans of the abdomen.  She worries that her previous physicians may have missed something.  The patient does not drink alcohol or use recreational substances.  Menstruation occurs every 30 days with no associated increase in abdominal pain.  Medications include a daily multivitamin and acetaminophen as needed for pain.  Medical history is otherwise noncontributory.  Vital signs are normal.  Physical examination shows no abnormalities.  The patient is cooperative and describes her mood as "okay."  There is no suicidal ideation.  Results of chemistry panel, complete blood count, and urinalysis are within normal limits and are shared with the patient.  Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​

explanation:
Somatic symptom disorder

Risk factors

  • Female
  • Lower educational level
  • Chronic childhood illness or family history of chronic illness
  • Sexual trauma

Key features

  • ≥1 somatic symptoms causing distress/functional impairment
  • Excessive thoughts, anxiety, or behaviors (time & energy) related to symptoms
  • ≥6-month duration

Associated features

  • High health care use/multiple providers
  • Repeated testing rarely reassuring

Management

  • Regularly scheduled visits (not symptom driven) with same provider
  • Limit unnecessary work-up & specialist referrals
  • Legitimize symptoms but focus on stress reduction & coping strategies
  • Antidepressants, cognitive-behavioral therapy if treatment resistant

This patient's preoccupation with unexplained medical symptoms despite multiple extensive, unremarkable evaluations suggests somatic symptom disorder (SSD).  This condition is characterized by pervasive thoughts and excessive concern about somatic symptoms, resulting in significant psychosocial distress.  Although not every patient with unexplained symptoms has SSD, the diagnosis should be considered after multiple work-ups for long-standing symptoms fail to reveal an etiology.

Optimal management involves regularly scheduled outpatient visits with the same medical provider (eg, primary care physician).  This approach allows patients to discuss their concerns without needing to have new or worsening symptoms.  Providers should acknowledge and legitimize symptoms while providing reassurance that serious conditions have been considered and ruled out.  Thoughtful justification about why additional testing is unnecessary can minimize overuse of health care resources.

Over time, the focus of visits can shift from discussion of physical symptoms to identification of psychologic stressors and coping strategies, with emphasis on stress reduction, healthy behaviors (eg, diet, exercise), and functional improvement (eg, return to occupational and social activities).  Patients can also be reassured that further evaluation will be considered if their typical symptoms suddenly change.

(Choice A)  This patient currently has limited insight into the psychologic nature of her disorder and would likely feel invalidated if told that her condition is psychogenic.  Once a patient-physician relationship is well established, she may be more receptive to the idea that psychologic distress has a role in her condition.

(Choice B)  This patient has undergone multiple extensive work-ups for her chronic symptoms.  There are no reported changes, so further work-up with MRI would not be helpful and could perpetuate health care overuse.

(Choice C)  Opioid analgesics are highly addictive and should be avoided in patients with ongoing pain of unclear etiology, particularly if a psychosomatic source is suspected.

(Choice D)  Cognitive-behavioral therapy may be helpful in patients whose conditions do not improve with regularly scheduled visits, but a referral must be made cautiously because patients can feel dismissed or misunderstood.  A strong patient-physician relationship should be established first.

Educational objective:Somatic symptom disorder involves pervasive thoughts, excessive concern, and psychologic distress about unexplained medical symptoms.  It is best managed with regularly scheduled outpatient visits that are not contingent on having active symptoms.  Providers should give reassurance and thoughtful justifications to reduce the overuse of health care resources.​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​
